standard_text: Use rational approximations of irrational numbers to compare the size of irrational numbers, plot them approximately on a number line, and estimate the value of expressions involving irrational numbers.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to approximate irrational numbers with nearby rationals so they can compare their sizes, plot them on a number line, and estimate expressions like the square root of 2 plus 3, all without a calculator. The on-grade work repeats one move: bracket a square root between the two perfect squares that hug it, lean toward the closer one, then use that estimate to place, compare, or select. Students who stall here usually lack the grade 7 groundwork, which is instant recall of perfect squares and their roots and comfort ordering rational numbers on a number line. Below that sit grade 4 and 5 gaps in multiplication facts and decimal comparison, where errors like 7 squared is 14 and more digits means bigger are born. Intervention rebuilds facts and decimal placement first, then perfect square roots and rational ordering, and only then returns to estimating irrationals.

steps.rationale: The entry approximation the whole standard rests on: replace an irrational square root with the nearest whole number by finding the perfect squares it sits between.
Turns the estimate into a position: place an irrational number at its approximate spot on a number line between two integers, leaning toward the closer end.
Names the bracket explicitly -- which two consecutive whole numbers a square root falls between -- the reasoning that powers every later comparison.
Applies the bracket to many numbers at once: decide which values, rational and irrational, fall inside a given range.
The At-proficiency target: compare an irrational number to a rational number using an approximation, stated as an inequality, a number line, or in words.
The Above-proficiency extension: approximate expressions that combine an irrational number with one operation, then compare their values.

skills.name: Multiply whole numbers fluently and build square numbers with arrays

prerequisite_skill.description: Recall multiplication facts through 12 x 12 and use an array to show a number times itself.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 7 x 7? How many tiles fill a 7 by 7 square?

skills.i_do_script: A multiplication fact counts equal rows. Watch: 7 x 7 means 7 rows with 7 tiles in each row. I build the square array and count: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49. So 7 x 7 = 49, not 14; 14 would be 7 + 7, only two rows. When the two factors match, the array is a perfect square shape, which is why numbers like 25, 36, and 49 are called square numbers. Knowing these facts cold is what makes every later square root question fast.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds or doubles instead of multiplying
canonical_error.why: The student reads times as plus. The array shows 7 rows of 7, which is 49 tiles; 14 tiles would make only 2 rows of 7.

skills.name: Compare decimals and place them on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare decimals to the hundredths by place value and place them on a number line marked in tenths.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Which is greater, 3.7 or 3.12? Where does 3.7 go on a line from 3 to 4?

skills.i_do_script: A longer decimal is not automatically a bigger number; the place values decide. Watch: to compare 3.7 and 3.12, I compare tenths first. 7 tenths beats 1 tenth, so 3.7 is greater even though 312 looks bigger than 37. On a number line from 3 to 4 marked in tenths, 3.7 sits at the seventh tick and 3.12 sits just past the first tick, so 3.7 is farther right. Money helps too: $3.70 is more than $3.12.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares decimals by digit count instead of place value
canonical_error.why: The student compares the digit strings instead of the places. Tenths are compared first, and 7 tenths is more than 1 tenth, so 3.7 is greater and sits farther right.

skills.name: Find square roots of perfect squares

prerequisite_skill.description: Know squaring and finding a square root are inverse operations, and find square roots of perfect squares through 225.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is the square root of 64? What is 9 squared?

skills.i_do_script: Squaring and finding a square root undo each other. Watch: 9 squared means 9 x 9, and a 9 by 9 tile square holds 81 tiles, so 9 squared is 81. The square root runs it backward: the square root of 81 asks what side length makes a square of 81 tiles, and the answer is 9. I am not halving; half of 81 is 40.5, and 40.5 x 40.5 is over 1600, nowhere near 81. I keep the perfect squares in a row I can recite: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100, 121, 144, 169, 196, 225.

canonical_error.pattern: Treats a square root as half the number
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 36 is 18 because 36 / 2 = 18
canonical_error.why: The student reads root as half because both make the number smaller. A square root asks what number times itself gives the value, and 6 x 6 = 36, so the root is 6. Check: 18 x 18 = 324, not 36.

skills.item_template: A perfect square through 225 to root, a whole number through 15 to square, or a yes/no perfect-square check. Short and multiple choice.

vocabulary.definition: A whole number equal to some whole number times itself, like 49 = 7 x 7.
The number that, multiplied by itself, gives the value; the square root of 25 is 5.

skills.name: Compare and order rational numbers on a number line

prerequisite_skill.description: Compare and order positive and negative fractions and decimals and place them on a number line.

skills.i_do_script: Every rational number has one spot on the number line, and farther right always means greater. Watch: to order -1.5, 3/4, -2, and 0.7, I turn each into a position. The negatives sit left of zero: -2 is farther left than -1.5, so -2 is least. On the right side, 3/4 is 0.75, which is a little past 0.7. So the order is -2, -1.5, 0.7, 3/4. Renaming a fraction as a decimal lets me place everything on the same line.

skills.name: Estimate a square root to the nearest whole number
skills.i_do_script: To estimate the square root of a number to the nearest whole number, I find the two perfect squares it lands between, then decide which one it is closer to. Watch the square root of 30. The perfect squares around 30 are 25 (5 x 5) and 36 (6 x 6), so the square root of 30 is between 5 and 6. Since 30 is closer to 25 than to 36, the square root of 30 is closer to 5 -- about 5.5, so to the nearest whole number it rounds to 5. I am NOT dividing 30 by 2; halving would give 15, which is way too big.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the number under the root by 2 instead of estimating the root
canonical_error.example: Says the square root of 30 is about 15 (30 / 2) instead of about 5
canonical_error.why: The student treats a square root like halving because both shrink the number. A square root asks which number times itself gives the value, so the square root of 30 is near 5.5, not 15.

skills.name: Approximate an irrational expression to the nearest tenth
skills.i_do_script: Nearest whole number was the easy version: find the two perfect squares it sits between and pick the closer one. Nearest tenth needs one more move. Watch the square root of 24. It sits between 16 and 25, so between 4 and 5, and 24 is much closer to 25, so I expect something near 4.9. I test it: 4.9 times 4.9 is 24.01. That is just past 24, so the square root of 24 is a hair under 4.9. To the nearest tenth, 4.9. And when there is an operation under the radical, that comes first -- always simplify inside before you estimate.

canonical_error.pattern: Applies the square root to only part of the radicand when an operation sits underneath it, or estimates before simplifying inside
canonical_error.example: For the square root of (3 squared plus 3), computes 3 plus the square root of 3, or takes the square root of 9 and then adds 3, instead of simplifying 9 plus 3 to 12 first
canonical_error.why: The radical bar is a grouping symbol, but it does not look like parentheses, so the student treats the terms under it as separate. Every prior square root had a single number underneath, so there was never an inside to simplify.

skills.item_template: An irrational value to approximate to the nearest tenth. Some items place an operation inside the radicand so the expression must be simplified before it is estimated. Multiple choice with tenth-place options, or numeric response.

sample_items.answer: About 7.4, because 7.4 times 7.4 is 54.76 and 7.5 times 7.5 is 56.25, so 55 sits nearer 7.4
sample_items.distractor_logic: Answering 7.5 without testing shows the midpoint was assumed rather than checked.

sample_items.stem: Approximate 2 times pi to the nearest tenth.

sample_items.distractor_logic: 6.2 comes from truncating rather than rounding; 3.1 comes from forgetting the coefficient.

redirect_script.stop: Is there an operation underneath that radical? Handle it before you estimate anything.
redirect_script.prompt: The radical bar groups everything under it, like parentheses. Simplify inside to a single number first. Then find the two perfect squares it sits between, and test a tenth by multiplying it by itself.
redirect_script.praise: You simplified inside first and then tested your tenth by squaring it. That is the whole method.

vocabulary.definition: Everything underneath the radical bar. It is grouped, so it gets simplified first.

A whole number that is some whole number times itself. They are the landmarks you estimate between.
A close value, not an exact one. Irrational numbers have no exact decimal.

worked_example_script.text: Write the square root of 24 on the board, and underneath it write 16 and 25 with a gap between them.
24 sits between which two perfect squares? So the answer sits between which two whole numbers?
Is 24 nearer 16 or nearer 25? So should our estimate be nearer 4 or nearer 5?
If a student says 4.5 because it is halfway, have them square it: 20.25. That is well short of 24, which shows the value sits higher than halfway. Let the test do the correcting.
Try 4.9. What is 4.9 times 4.9? We got 24.01 -- just past 24. What does that tell us?
New one: the square root of (3 squared plus 3). Before we estimate anything, what has to happen underneath the bar?
9 plus 3 is 12. Now the square root of 12 -- between which whole numbers, and nearer which one?
Simplify inside, find the two landmarks, then test a tenth by squaring it. The squaring is what turns a guess into an estimate.

printable_artifact.title: Estimate to the Tenth
printable_artifact.instructions: Three moves, in this order. Never estimate before you simplify inside.
items: 1. SIMPLIFY under the bar. The radical groups everything beneath it.
2. LANDMARK: find the perfect squares on either side.
3. TEST a tenth: multiply it by itself and compare to the target.
sqrt(24): between 16 and 25, so between 4 and 5. 4.9 x 4.9 = 24.01, so about 4.9.
k x pi: use pi about 3.14, then multiply. 2pi is about 6.3.

practice_problems.stem: Read Kwame's work. Find his mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Approximate the square root of (5 squared plus 11) to the nearest tenth.
Kwame wrote: 'The square root of 5 squared is 5. So this is 5 plus the square root of 11, which is about 5 + 3.3 = 8.3.'
practice_problems.answer: About 6.0. Kwame split the radicand, but the radical bar groups everything underneath it, so the inside has to be simplified first: 5 squared plus 11 is 25 plus 11, which is 36. The square root of 36 is exactly 6. A square root does not distribute across addition -- his method would also claim the square root of (9 plus 16) is 3 plus 4, which is 7, when it is really the square root of 25, which is 5.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error, and the counterexample at the end is worth running with the class -- it makes the non-distribution concrete.

practice_problems.stem: Approximate 2 times pi to the nearest tenth, and explain why your method differs from estimating a square root.
practice_problems.answer: About 6.3, since pi is roughly 3.14 and 2 x 3.14 = 6.28. It differs because pi has a known decimal approximation to start from, so there is nothing to squeeze between landmarks -- you multiply and round.

practice_problems.stem: Without a calculator, decide which is larger: the square root of 40 or 6.3. Justify with a multiplication.
practice_problems.answer: The square root of 40 is larger. Check by squaring: 6.3 x 6.3 = 39.69, which falls short of 40, so the square root of 40 must be slightly greater than 6.3 (it is about 6.32).
practice_problems.notes: Deliberately requires the squaring test rather than intuition; students who guess get it backwards.

activities.title: Squeeze to the Tenth
activities.instructions:
1. Post a non-perfect square such as 24, 40, or 55.
2. Partner A names the two whole-number landmarks and marks them.
3. Partner B picks a tenth between them and squares it on the whiteboard.
4. Compare the square to the target and slide the marker up or down. Repeat until two neighbouring tenths straddle the target.
5. Record the nearer one. Run at least one item with an operation under the radical so the simplify-first step gets practised.

activities.title: Kwame Split the Radical
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Kwame's work and compute the correct value before discussing his method.
2. Ask first: why is splitting tempting? (It looks like distributing, which works for multiplication.)
3. Pairs test his method on the square root of (9 plus 16), where the answer is checkable: his way gives 7, the correct way gives 5.
4. Pairs write one sentence about what the radical bar does to the terms underneath it.

content.worked_problem: Approximate the square root of (5 squared plus 11). Kwame wrote: 'sqrt(5 squared) is 5, so this is 5 + sqrt(11), about 8.3.'
content.error_step: Kwame split the radical across an addition instead of simplifying the radicand first.
content.why: The radical bar groups everything beneath it. 25 plus 11 is 36, and the square root of 36 is exactly 6. Testing his method on sqrt(9 + 16) exposes it: he would get 7 where the true value is 5.

activities.title: Higher or Lower, Squared
activities.instructions:
1. Post a target such as the square root of 47.
2. Students write a tenth-place guess and square it.
3. Reveal squares around the group: anyone whose square is above the target says HIGHER, below says LOWER.
4. Round two: everyone must guess between the closest HIGHER and closest LOWER from round one.
5. Two rounds is usually enough to pin the tenth. Debrief on why squaring is faster than guessing.

strategy_links.why: The tenth-marked number line plus the squaring check keeps estimation concrete instead of a remembered decimal.
Kwame's split radical is the canonical error, and it is checkable against a case with an exact answer.
Squaring tenths mentally to narrow an interval is exactly the kind of reasoning a number talk builds.

skills.name: Select all numbers within a given range
skills.i_do_script: Sometimes I'm given a range and a list of numbers -- some rational, some irrational -- and must pick every one that lands inside. I estimate each value, then check if it is greater than the low end and less than the high end. Watch: greater than 1.5 and less than 5. The square root of 10 is about 3.2 (in), 4.5 is in, the square root of 30 is about 5.5 (out, too big), and 1 is out (too small). I keep the halving trap in mind: the square root of 30 is about 5.5, not 15.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges an irrational number against the range using the radicand or half of it instead of its estimate
canonical_error.example: For 'greater than 1.5 and less than 5,' excludes the square root of 10 by treating it as 10 (too big) though it is about 3.2 and belongs in the range
canonical_error.why: The square root of 10 must first be estimated to about 3.2 before comparing; using 10 (the radicand) or 5 (halving) puts it on the wrong side of the range.

skills.name: Name a number that meets a given comparison requirement
skills.i_do_script: Until now you were handed numbers and asked to compare them. Now you are handed a condition and asked to produce a number that satisfies it. Watch: name an irrational number between 5 and 6. I need a square root landing in that stretch, so I need a radicand between 25 and 36 that is not a perfect square. 30 works, so the square root of 30 works. And so does the square root of 27, and the square root of 31. Many answers, all correct, and I can check every one by squaring the bounds.

canonical_error.pattern: Produces a number that satisfies the interval but not the rational-or-irrational requirement, most often by naming a perfect square root or a terminating decimal when an irrational is asked for
canonical_error.example: Asked for an irrational number between 5 and 6, answers 5.5, or answers the square root of 25 because it 'looks irrational'
canonical_error.why: The student attends to the interval, which is the visible constraint, and treats the word irrational as decoration. The square root symbol reads as a signal for irrational regardless of what sits under it, so sqrt(25) passes their check even though it equals 5.

skills.item_template: A condition rather than a question: an interval plus a number-type requirement (rational or irrational), or a comparison to satisfy. The student produces a value and justifies that it meets every part of the condition. Open response with many correct answers.

sample_items.stem: Name an irrational number between 5 and 6. Justify that your number satisfies both requirements.
sample_items.answer: Any square root of a non-perfect square between 25 and 36, e.g. the square root of 30. It is between 5 and 6 because 25 < 30 < 36, and it is irrational because 30 is not a perfect square.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5.5 satisfies the interval but is rational; sqrt(25) is neither irrational nor strictly between.

sample_items.stem: Name a rational number between the square root of 7 and the square root of 11.
sample_items.answer: Any terminating decimal between about 2.65 and about 3.32, for example 3
sample_items.distractor_logic: Naming another square root satisfies the interval but not the rational requirement.

sample_items.stem: Name a number greater than 3 times pi.
sample_items.answer: Any value above about 9.42, for example 10
sample_items.distractor_logic: Answering 9 shows pi was rounded down to 3 rather than approximated to 3.14.

sample_items.stem: Is it possible to name an irrational number between 4 and 4.1? Explain.
sample_items.answer: Yes. Any square root of a non-perfect square between 16 and 16.81 works, such as the square root of 16.5. Narrow intervals still contain infinitely many irrational numbers.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Saying no treats the interval's width as the limit rather than the density of the reals.

redirect_script.stop: Read the condition back to me. How many requirements are in it?

redirect_script.praise: You checked both requirements, not just the one you could see on the number line.

vocabulary.definition: A number whose decimal never ends and never repeats. Square roots of non-perfect squares, and pi, are irrational.
A number that can be written as a fraction of integers. Terminating and repeating decimals are rational.
A requirement an answer must satisfy. A problem may state more than one at once.
A whole number that is not any whole number times itself. Its square root is irrational.

skills.name: Estimate and compare values of expressions involving irrational numbers
skills.i_do_script: To compare expressions that include an irrational number, I estimate the irrational part, do the one operation, then compare. Watch: is the square root of 2 + 3 greater than 4? The square root of 2 is about 1.4, so the square root of 2 + 3 is about 4.4, which is greater than 4 -- true. For 3 times pi, I use pi is about 3.14, so 3 times pi is about 9.4. I estimate the irrational piece to a decimal, then finish the arithmetic; I never treat the square root of 2 as 1 (rounding too hard) or halving it.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops or over-rounds the irrational part before doing the operation
canonical_error.example: Estimates the square root of 2 + 3 as 4 by calling the square root of 2 equal to 1, instead of about 1.4 for a value near 4.4
canonical_error.why: The student replaces the irrational number with a whole number that is too rough (or halves it), so the expression's estimate is off by enough to flip a comparison.

skills.name: Order a mixed set of rational and irrational numbers and justify the order
skills.i_do_script: A list with square roots, decimals, whole numbers, and multiples of pi cannot be sorted by looking. Every value has to be converted into the same currency first, and that currency is a decimal approximation. Watch: 3pi, sqrt(35), 7.4, sqrt(50), 9. I approximate every single one before I move anything. 3pi is about 9.42, sqrt(35) is about 5.9, 7.4 is 7.4, sqrt(50) is about 7.07, 9 is 9. Now the order is obvious. The approximating is the work; the sorting is the easy part.

canonical_error.pattern: Sorts by the radicand or the coefficient rather than by the value of the expression, so large numbers under a radical are placed as though they were large numbers
canonical_error.example: Orders sqrt(35) after 9 because 35 is greater than 9, or places 3pi below 7.4 because 3 is less than 7
canonical_error.why: The student compares the symbols they can read directly instead of what the expression evaluates to. The radicand and the coefficient are the visible numbers, and nothing on the page announces that sqrt(35) is smaller than 6.

skills.item_template: A list of four to six values mixing rational and irrational forms, to be ordered least to greatest, plus a written justification explaining how the comparison was made. Two-part response; the justification is assessed separately from the ordering.

sample_items.stem: Order from least to greatest: 3pi, the square root of 35, 7.4, the square root of 50, 9. Then justify your ordering by explaining how you compared the rational and irrational values.
sample_items.answer: sqrt(35) (about 5.92), sqrt(50) (about 7.07), 7.4, 9, 3pi (about 9.42). Every value was approximated as a decimal so they could be compared on one scale.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Placing sqrt(50) or sqrt(35) last comes from ordering by radicand; placing 3pi first comes from ordering by coefficient.

sample_items.stem: Order from least to greatest: 2pi, 6, the square root of 40, 6.5.
sample_items.distractor_logic: These four are deliberately close together, so estimating to the nearest whole number is not precise enough to separate them.

sample_items.stem: Jonah ordered sqrt(20), 4.5, and sqrt(17) as sqrt(17), sqrt(20), 4.5. Is he correct? Justify.
sample_items.answer: Yes, Jonah is correct. sqrt(17) is about 4.12, sqrt(20) is about 4.47, and 4.5 is greater than both, so his order is right. Not every critique item contains an error.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who expect every critique item to contain an error will invent one.

sample_items.stem: Which is larger, the square root of 80 or 3pi? Justify with approximations.
sample_items.answer: 3pi. The square root of 80 is about 8.94 and 3pi is about 9.42.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Comparing 80 to 3 makes the square root look much larger.

redirect_script.praise: You approximated everything before sorting anything. That is why the ordering came out right the first time.

vocabulary.definition: A close decimal value used so different forms can be compared on one scale.
Explain how you knew, not just what you decided.
The number under the radical. Its size is not the size of the expression.
The multiplier in front, as the 3 in 3pi.

skills.manipulative_visual: Index cards each showing an expression on the front and its decimal approximation on the back. Students order face-down by approximation, then flip the whole row to reveal the original expressions in sorted order, which makes the conversion step visibly load-bearing.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8NS2-S6: estimate and compare expressions built from irrational values, where the ordering has to be judged without exact decimals.
next_steps.if_fail: Drop back to 8NS2-S7 and rebuild tenth-place approximation, then return here with lists of three before moving to five.

worked_example_script.text: Write on the board, spaced far apart: 3pi, sqrt(35), 7.4, sqrt(50), 9. Leave a blank line above each.
Could I sort these by looking at them? What makes that hard?
Let's convert everything first. What is sqrt(35) worth, roughly? Which perfect squares does 35 sit between?
If a student starts moving values before all five are approximated, stop and ask what sqrt(50) is worth. Sorting a value you have not converted is where the error enters.
3pi -- what do we use for pi, and what does that give us?
All five approximated. Now read me the order, least to greatest.
Look at 9 and 3pi. Why would someone put 9 last if they sorted by the numbers they could see?
Approximate everything, then sort. And the justification has to say that -- the reasoning is what is being assessed, not just the row.

printable_artifact.instructions: Never sort a value you have not converted. Approximate all of them, then order.
items: sqrt(n): find the perfect squares either side, estimate to a tenth.
k x pi: use pi about 3.14, multiply.
Decimals and whole numbers: already in decimal form.
3pi is about 9.42.  sqrt(35) is about 5.92.  sqrt(50) is about 7.07.
The RADICAND is not the value: sqrt(35) is smaller than 9, even though 35 is bigger.
The justification must say HOW you compared, not just the final order.

practice_problems.stem: Approximate the square root of 35 to the nearest tenth.
practice_problems.answer: About 5.9

practice_problems.stem: Approximate 3 times pi.
practice_problems.answer: About 9.42

practice_problems.stem:
A list of numbers is given: 3pi, the square root of 35, 7.4, the square root of 50, 9.
Part A: Order the numbers from least to greatest.
Part B: Justify your ordering by explaining how you compared the rational and irrational values.
practice_problems.answer: Part A: sqrt(35), sqrt(50), 7.4, 9, 3pi. Part B: each value was approximated as a decimal first -- sqrt(35) about 5.92, sqrt(50) about 7.07, 7.4 exactly, 9 exactly, 3pi about 9.42 -- so all five could be compared on the same scale.
practice_problems.notes: The spec's own above-proficiency item. Part B is assessed separately; an ordering with no method earns half.

practice_problems.stem: Order from least to greatest: 2pi, 6, the square root of 40, 6.5.
practice_problems.answer: 6, 2pi (about 6.28), sqrt(40) (about 6.32), 6.5
practice_problems.notes: Deliberately tight. Nearest-whole-number estimates cannot separate 2pi from sqrt(40) -- tenths are required.

practice_problems.stem: Which is larger, the square root of 80 or 3 times pi? Justify with approximations.
practice_problems.answer: 3pi is larger: sqrt(80) is about 8.94 and 3pi is about 9.42.
practice_problems.notes: Comparing 80 against 3 makes the root look far bigger, which is the trap.

practice_problems.stem: Read Lena's ordering. Decide whether it is correct and explain.
shown_work: Task: order from least to greatest -- sqrt(30), 5.6, 4pi, 6.
Lena wrote: '5.6, 6, 4pi, sqrt(30), because 30 is the biggest number in the list and 4 is the smallest.'
practice_problems.answer: Lena's order is wrong. She sorted by the numbers she could read rather than by value. Approximating: sqrt(30) is about 5.48, 5.6 is 5.6, 4pi is about 12.57, and 6 is 6. The correct order is sqrt(30), 5.6, 6, 4pi. The radicand 30 is not the size of sqrt(30), and the coefficient 4 is not the size of 4pi.
practice_problems.notes: The canonical error in both directions at once -- radicand too big, coefficient too small.

practice_problems.stem: Build a list of four numbers -- at least one square root, at least one multiple of pi, and at least one decimal -- whose correct order is the exact reverse of the order they would take if someone sorted by the visible numbers. Trade with a partner.
practice_problems.answer: Answers vary. For example sqrt(80), 2pi, 9.5, 3: sorting by visible numbers gives 2pi, 3, sqrt(80), 9.5, while true order is 3, 2pi (about 6.28), sqrt(80) (about 8.94), 9.5.
practice_problems.notes: Constructing the trap requires understanding it from both sides.

practice_problems.stem: Two students order a list correctly but justify it differently. One writes 'I approximated each value to a decimal and compared.' The other writes 'I just knew.' Both orders are right. Should they earn the same credit? Explain what a justification has to contain.
practice_problems.answer: No. The task asks for the ordering and the reasoning, so a justification must name the method: converting every value to a decimal approximation so the forms can be compared on one scale. 'I just knew' gives the reader nothing to check and would not survive a harder list.

activities.title: Flip the Row
materials: Index cards with an expression on the front and space on the back
activities.instructions:
1. Each group gets five cards showing mixed forms.
2. Groups write the decimal approximation on the BACK of each card, one at a time, with no sorting yet.
3. Turn all cards approximation-side up and order the row.
4. Flip the whole row to reveal the original expressions in sorted order.
5. Debrief: which card's position was most surprising, and what would you have guessed from the front alone?

activities.title: Lena Sorted What She Could See
activities.instructions:
1. Pairs read Lena's order and her reason before checking anything.
2. Pairs approximate all four values and write each above its expression.
3. Pairs identify both of Lena's errors -- the radicand read as a value, and the coefficient read as a value.
4. Pairs write a corrected order plus a one-sentence justification naming the method.

content.worked_problem: Order sqrt(30), 5.6, 4pi, 6 from least to greatest. Lena wrote 5.6, 6, 4pi, sqrt(30), reasoning that 30 is largest and 4 is smallest.
content.error_step: Lena ordered by the visible numbers -- the radicand and the coefficient -- instead of by the value each expression represents.
content.why: Approximating gives sqrt(30) about 5.48, 5.6, 6, and 4pi about 12.57, so the correct order is sqrt(30), 5.6, 6, 4pi. The number under a radical shrinks when the root is taken; the number in front of pi multiplies.

activities.title: Insert the Card
materials: A pre-ordered row of expression cards on the board
activities.instructions:
1. Post four expressions already in correct order with gaps between them.
2. Hand a student a new card. They must place it in the correct gap and state its approximation aloud.
3. The class votes before the placement is confirmed.
4. A correct placement with no approximation stated does not score -- the method is the point.
5. Finish with a card that lands between two very close neighbours so tenths matter.

strategy_links.why: Part B of these items is written reasoning, so composing the justification in words is the assessed product.
Lena's ordering carries the canonical error in both directions and is checkable by approximation.
The flip-the-row cards make the conversion step physically prior to the sorting step.

questioning_prompts: What is every value on that list worth as a decimal? Write them all before you move anything.
Is the number under the radical the same as the value of the expression?
Your order is right. Now what does your justification tell a reader about HOW you compared?
Which two values on this list are closest? Are your approximations precise enough to separate them?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student orders by radicand or by coefficient.
misconception_redirects.say: Convert every value to a decimal approximation first, and write each one above its expression. You cannot compare a radicand to a coefficient to a decimal. Get them into the same currency, then sort.
misconception_redirects.praise: You approximated everything before sorting anything. That is why the ordering came out right the first time.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student produces a correct order with a justification of 'I just knew.'
misconception_redirects.say: Part B asks how you compared. Write the sentence a reader could follow to get the same order.
misconception_redirects.praise: That justification names the method. Someone could repeat your reasoning on a different list.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student rounds everything to whole numbers and cannot separate two close values.
misconception_redirects.say: Those two rounded to the same whole number. Go one decimal place further and compare again.
misconception_redirects.praise: Good -- precision matched to how close the values actually are.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, naming the two consecutive whole numbers that bracket a square root, the move the whole standard rests on. If they pass, move up to S5 (compare an irrational number to a rational one) and S6 (estimate expressions). If they fail, drop one grade: B1 checks square roots of perfect squares and B2 checks ordering rational numbers on a number line, the two grade 7 skills bracketing leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (multiplication facts and square arrays, grade 4) and F2 (decimal comparison and placement, grade 5) locate the gap. S1, S2, and S4 remain available to probe estimating, plotting, and range selection on grade level.

pld_descriptors.note: Verbatim from the ILEARN item specification. These are performance bands on THIS standard, not lower-grade content: a student at Below Proficiency is working on this standard at its least complex entry point.
pld_descriptors.below: Plot rational approximations of irrational numbers on a number line. Identify an irrational number that is greater than or less than a given whole number. Identify the approximate value to the nearest whole number of an irrational number.
pld_descriptors.approaching: Identify approximated values of irrational numbers to the nearest tenth, including those with a numerical operation in the radicand, requiring simplification prior to approximation. Compare irrational numbers within intervals.
pld_descriptors.at: Compare a rational number and a rational approximation of an irrational number using inequalities, number lines, or verbal statements. Determine rational and/or irrational numbers that meet given comparison requirements.
pld_descriptors.above: Analyze and compare values using rational approximations of complex irrational expressions and large non-perfect square radicals. Order sets of rational and irrational numbers from least to greatest and justify comparisons.
